title: Many streams
hook: modern Jews organize themselves in movements; no single one speaks for all

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the block on Kabbalah and Hasidism with the hidden light: the light of the first day, put away and sown for the righteous. Did something ordinary catch the light? Today, a new block. Day one thousand two hundred eleven.

Three Jewish friends walk into a coffee shop on a Saturday morning. Well, two of them do. The third is at synagogue, and won't use his phone until Shabbat ends, so the group chat will have to wait. One of the two in the coffee shop is heading to her own synagogue later, where the prayers mix Hebrew and English. The other one lights candles on Friday night and calls herself just Jewish, no label. All three are telling the truth. Today's word is the map that helps you see all three at once.
screen: `SATURDAY MORNING, A COFFEE SHOP.` → `ONE AT SYNAGOGUE, PHONE OFF.` → `ALL THREE TELLING THE TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Many streams. In modern Hebrew, the movements are often called zeramim, streams. Turn it four ways. First, the names. Orthodox Judaism, which itself holds many communities, from Modern Orthodox to Haredi, including the Hasidic courts we just met. Conservative Judaism, called Masorti in Israel and elsewhere. Reform Judaism. Reconstructionist Judaism. And others, like Jewish Renewal, which Reb Zalman helped begin. Second, what divides them. Mostly, questions like these: how Jewish law binds today, who has the authority to decide, and how tradition meets modern life. They answer differently, and sometimes they disagree sharply about each other. Third, what the map leaves out. Some Sephardi and Mizrahi communities don't sort neatly into these labels. Some Jews belong to no movement at all, and some move between them over a lifetime. A label tells you something about a synagogue. It tells you less about a person. Fourth, the old argument. The Talmud tells of the schools of Hillel and Shammai, who argued for years until a voice from heaven said: these and these are the words of the living God, and the law follows Hillel. Some people today reach for that line to describe the movements. Others say it was about two schools inside one law and doesn't stretch that far. That disagreement is itself part of the map. And here's the rule for this whole block: no single movement speaks for all Jews, and this path won't rank them. The Psalm has a picture for it: "There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God." Now look back over this week. A ladder of song. Women of the court. Hasidism beyond the court. Two paths inward. Mystic kindness. The hidden light. And today, many streams.
screen: `ORTHODOX, CONSERVATIVE, REFORM …` · `HOW DOES THE LAW BIND?` · `A LABEL TELLS YOU LESS.` · `THESE AND THESE.` · then, large: `MANY STREAMS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one movement's name, slowly. Settle, and breathe. Choose one name from today: Orthodox, Conservative, Reform, Reconstructionist or Renewal. If you're Jewish, it can be your own, or one you've never visited. Say it quietly. Then ask: what do I actually know about it? And what have I only assumed? Let the assumptions go by like water. Keep only what you know, and the wish to learn more. After the bell, if you like, look up how that movement describes itself, in its own words. The bell holds the time.
Many streams. The movements of modern Jewish life, Orthodox, Conservative, Reform, Reconstructionist and others, none of which speaks for all Jews. Today's word.
Your line: many streams. Today, if you meet a label, a Jewish one or any other, ask what the person means by it before you decide what it means. Day one thousand two hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Jews may belong to a synagogue affiliated with a movement, such as Orthodox, Conservative or Masorti, Reform, Reconstructionist or Renewal, or to an independent or Sephardi community, or to none; each movement has its own seminaries, prayer books and understanding of Jewish law.

fork.setup: a new friend tells you she's Jewish. what can you assume about how she keeps Shabbat?
options: she doesn't keep it at all.
fork.reveal: a label tells you something about a synagogue and less about a person. the coffee shop friends were all telling the truth.

original.note: Hebrew: a stream or current; in modern Hebrew, also a movement within Judaism (plural zeramim).

trapdoor: what you thought: Jews are all the same, or else split into rival sects.
what it means: modern Jews organize in movements, none of which speaks for all, and some Jews fit none.
what a scholar hears: Eruvin 13b's "these and these", and the live debate over whether it stretches to today's movements.
recall: the Yiddish way of saying rabbi

notes: Psalm 46:4 is KJV numbering (46:5 in Hebrew Bibles and JPS 1917).

Eruvin 13b paraphrased ('these and these are the words of the living God, and the law follows Hillel'); the Talmud's 'three years' detail is left out per the claims rule. The script notes that applying it to modern movements is itself disputed; please confirm this is fair to Orthodox readers.
'Zeramim' as the modern Hebrew term for movements: please confirm.
'Some Sephardi and Mizrahi communities...' and 'some Jews belong to no movement' are kept soft without statistics; please confirm wording.
Hook's Reform-style service 'with a guitar and mostly in English' is one illustrative synagogue, not a description of a movement; please confirm it doesn't read as a stereotype.
